title: Island / Landmass Context: What Island Am I On?
description: Click a point to read its island or mainland context with the Island / Landmass Context tool — place names that reveal the landmass. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, a point on Long Island answers with the island in its record — while a point ten miles north across the Sound is mainland, and the difference structures ferries, weather and house prices.
quick_answer: The Island / Landmass Context tool reads a clicked point's place record for names that indicate island or mainland context, and reports what the record holds. Click the point and read the address and place fields — a quick answer to 'what island is this?' from the map's own vocabulary.
steps_intro: The map names landmasses if you ask its record properly:

body.t: “Are we on an island here?” decides ferry bookings and bridge tolls. The record's answer is instant — the
A geotagged point from a boat trip resolves to its island name in the record, ready for the album.
Island addresses behave differently (delivery, evacuation, tides). The context read flags islandhood before those surprises.
Every coastline raises the question. The tool's modest method — read the record's names — is honest about how it knows.
Great islands announce themselves in every address field. Tiny islets may appear in no field at all — the tool's honesty: named context where names exist, silence where they do not.
Islands are not only coastal: the record treats river islands by their place names too, which is why a point in a wide river can answer 'island'.

faq: No — the record names what mappers recorded. Small islets, rocks and unnamed land may carry no place name, and the tool reports only what the fields hold rather than guessing.
Can I use the tool without sharing my precise location?
Yes — click any point on the map.
Why might a boundary or place name look different elsewhere?
Place naming is local and layered; other sources may use other names or languages for the same landmass.
Does MapBench store my browser location?
The fields usually settle it through names; ambiguous coastal points can read either way in sparse records. The map view is your tie-breaker.
A mid-ocean point may have no landmass record at all — which is itself the answer, of a wetter kind.
Places like tidal causeway islands carry island names in their records — context yes, tide tables no; check those separately before driving across.
The clicked point's reverse-geocode place and address fields from open map data — the same family of records as Coordinates to Address.
Where the record carries the group (the wider archipelago), it appears in the fields — the tool shows the record rather than choosing between island and group.
